title: IYT International Crew
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the IYT International Crew syllabus. Not official IYT exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

questions.q: A motor yacht is keeping pace with you, as shown. How do you tell the skipper where it is?
options: Abeam to starboard
On the starboard quarter
On the starboard bow
Abeam to port
questions.why: Abeam is at right angles to the boat; starboard is the right-hand side, facing forward.

questions.q: Snorkelling under the boat at anchor, you find a plastic bag wrapped round the blade right aft, just behind the propeller. What is it caught on?
options: The bow thruster
The rudder
The keel
The depth transducer
questions.why: The rudder is the steering blade at the stern, just behind the propeller.

questions.q: A guest from the next boat asks if they may use your heads. Where do you take them?
options: To the forepeak locker
To the chart table
To the toilet compartment
To the galley
questions.why: On a boat the toilet is called the heads.

questions.q: After a bumpy crossing the skipper asks you to check the bilge. Where do you look?
options: In the cockpit lockers under the seats
In the anchor locker at the bow
In the fresh-water tank under a berth
Under the saloon floorboards, at the lowest point
questions.why: The bilge is the lowest part inside the hull, where any water collects.

questions.q: The skipper asks you where the wind is coming from, relative to the boat. What do you answer?
options: Over the starboard quarter
Over the port quarter
Over the starboard bow
From dead astern
questions.why: The quarter lies between abeam and astern; here the wind comes from aft on the right-hand side.

questions.q: You have just cleared into Turkey and the skipper hands you the Turkish courtesy flag. Where do you hoist it?
options: On the stern flagstaff
Under the starboard spreader
At the top of the forestay
Under the port spreader
questions.why: A courtesy flag flies under the starboard spreader; the stern is for your own ensign.

questions.q: Entering a shallow bay, the skipper asks you to watch the depth sounder. Which figure tells you how much depth the boat needs?
options: The freeboard
The beam
The draft
The LOA
questions.why: Draft is how far the keel reaches below the waterline.

questions.q: The marina office asks for the boat's size to find you a berth between two other yachts. Which two figures do they need?
options: Draft and freeboard
Beam and freeboard
LOA and draft
LOA and beam
questions.why: A berth between boats must fit the overall length and the width (beam).

questions.q: Waves are starting to slop into the cockpit and the skipper asks you to put the washboards in. Which opening do they close?
options: The companionway into the cabin
The forward hatch over the berth
The cockpit drains
The anchor locker at the bow
questions.why: Washboards slot into the companionway so water in the cockpit cannot pour below.

questions.q: Before a windy crossing, the skipper asks you to check the wires that hold the mast up from the sides for broken strands. Which do you check?
options: The halyards
The shrouds
The backstay
The forestay
questions.why: Shrouds support the mast sideways; the forestay and backstay hold it fore and aft.

questions.q: Motoring slowly into a sandy bay, you feel a soft bump from below and the boat stops. Which part has most likely touched the bottom?
options: The bow at the waterline
The propeller blades
The bottom of the keel
The top of the rudder
questions.why: The keel is the deepest part of the boat; draft is measured to its bottom.

questions.q: The skipper says: "We'll anchor in the lee of the island tonight." Which spot does she mean?

figure.note: Wind N 20 kn, sea from the north

options: A or C, whichever is closer
C, on the west side
A, on the north side
B, on the south side
questions.why: The lee is the side sheltered from the wind: with a north wind, the south side.

questions.q: You come back in the tender. The yacht's sides are high, and it has a low bathing platform at the stern. Where do you climb aboard?
options: At the stern, where the freeboard is lowest
At the bow, holding on to the forestay
At the bow, up the anchor chain
Amidships, over the top of the guardrail
questions.why: Freeboard is the height of the deck above the water; board where it is lowest.

questions.q: As you approach the berth, the skipper calls: "Two crew aft, please!" Where do you go?
options: Towards the bow
Towards the stern
Down below to the saloon
To the mast
questions.why: Aft means towards the stern; forward means towards the bow.

questions.q: You come on deck at night and see the boom eased out over the starboard side. Which side is windward?
options: Starboard: the side the boat heels to
Starboard: the boom points into the wind
Port: the boom goes out to leeward
You cannot tell without a compass
questions.why: The wind pushes the boom away from it, so the boom is always on the leeward side.

questions.q: You are helping to unfurl the genoa. Which wire is the sail rolled round?
options: The backstay, from the stern up the mast
A shroud, from the side deck up the mast
The main halyard, inside the mast
The forestay, from the bow up the mast
questions.why: A roller-furling genoa rolls up round the forestay at the bow.

questions.q: The skipper asks how much water there is under the keel. What do you answer?

figure.title: Depth sounder
lines: Set to show depth below the waterline

options: About 0.5 m
About 2.1 m
About 4.7 m
About 2.6 m
questions.why: 2.6 m below the waterline minus 2.1 m of draft leaves 0.5 m under the keel.

questions.q: With the wind as shown, the skipper asks you to sit on the windward side, and later to tip a bucket of washing-up water over the side. Which sides do you use?
options: Sit to port; tip the bucket to starboard
Sit to starboard; tip the bucket to port
Sit to starboard; tip it to starboard
Sit to port; tip the bucket to port
questions.why: Windward is the side the wind comes from (starboard); anything thrown out goes to leeward.

questions.q: You spot this while going forward. What do you do?

figure.title: Under way, port tack
lines: Wind 18 kn over the port side
Skipper plans to tack in 10 minutes

options: Wait for the tack, then take a closer look
Mention it in harbour this evening
Tell the skipper before the tack: it takes the load then
Nothing: that shroud is slack, so it is safe
questions.why: After the tack the starboard shroud is to windward and holds the mast up; a loose fitting can fail.

questions.q: You are sitting in the cockpit facing aft, towards the stern. The skipper asks you to hang a fender on the port side. Which side is that from where you sit?
options: The side the wind comes from
Whichever side faces the quay
Your left-hand side
Your right-hand side
questions.why: Port and starboard belong to the boat, seen facing forward; facing aft, port is on your right.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to name this point of sail for the logbook. What is it?
options: Broad reach
Beam reach
Run
Close reach
questions.why: With the wind about 135° off the bow, over the quarter, you are on a broad reach.

questions.q: The helm turns onto this heading. The sails flap and the boat slows to a stop. Why?
options: The genoa has been furled too far
The boat is pointing into the no-go zone
The sheets are pulled in too tight
The wind has suddenly dropped
questions.why: No sail can drive the boat within about 45° of the wind: the no-go zone.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to "ease the main". Which line do you let out?
options: The main halyard
The genoa furling line
The mainsheet
The genoa sheet
questions.why: The mainsheet sets the angle of the boom; easing it lets the sail out.

questions.q: You are trimming the genoa on a steady reach. How do you find the right setting for the sheet?
options: Pull in until the tell-tales droop, then leave it
Ease until the whole sail flaps, then cleat it there
Pull in until the sail is hard and flat, then cleat it
Ease until the luff just flaps, then pull in enough to stop it
questions.why: The best trim is just short of luffing: ease till it flaps, then sheet in a touch.

questions.q: You are trimming the genoa and see this on the tell-tales. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa tell-tales
lines: Close reach, helm on a steady course

options: Pull the sheet in a little
Ease the sheet out a little
Leave it: the trim is right
Ease the genoa halyard a little
questions.why: A lifting windward tell-tale means the sail is eased too far: sheet in.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to sort out the genoa trim. What do you do with the sheet?
options: Pull it in a little
Ease it a little
Let it fly right out
Cleat it and leave it
questions.why: A drooping leeward tell-tale means the sail is stalled, sheeted too hard: ease it.

questions.q: In a tack you are on the new genoa sheet. As the genoa blows across, what do you do?
options: Wait until the sail fills, then start winding
Winch it in from the start, with all turns on
Pull the slack in fast by hand, then winch the last part
Wait until the old sheet has been coiled
questions.why: Slack comes in fastest by hand before the sail fills; the winch takes the last, loaded part.

questions.q: The helm calls "Ready to gybe". You are on the mainsheet. What do you do?
options: Cleat it where it is and keep well clear of the boom
Let the mainsheet run free so the boom can swing across
Ease it out further to spill the wind from the sail first
Pull the main in to the centre, then ease it on the new side
questions.why: Hauling the boom in first keeps its swing short and controlled; then ease it out.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to furl the genoa. What do you do with the furling line and the sheet?
options: Pull the furling line; ease the sheet with some tension
Pull the furling line; let the sheet fly free
Pull the sheet; ease the furling line slowly
Pull the genoa halyard; ease the sheet
questions.why: Light tension on the sheet rolls the sail up tightly and stops it flogging.

questions.q: You are unfurling the genoa in a fresh breeze. What do you do with the furling line?
options: Pull it in to help the sail start turning
Ease it out under control, with a turn round a winch
Cleat it firmly before you pull the sheet
Let it go completely so the sail opens fast
questions.why: A furling line let go runs wild and tangles on the drum; ease it with a turn on.

questions.q: The boat is head to wind and you are about to hoist the main. Which line must be eased before you pull the halyard?
options: The topping lift
The genoa sheet
The mainsheet
The genoa furling line
questions.why: A tight mainsheet holds the boom and leech down, so the sail cannot go up freely.

questions.q: Halfway up, the main fills with wind and the halyard suddenly becomes very heavy. What do you ask the helm?
options: To bear away so the sail fills properly
To speed up so the halyard runs easier
To tack so the sail moves across
To bring the bow back head to wind
questions.why: With the bow head to wind the main hangs empty and slides up easily.

questions.q: Why does the instrument show a breeze?

figure.title: Motoring in a flat calm
lines: Wind instrument: 6 kn from dead ahead
Sea glassy, flags ashore hanging limp

options: It is apparent wind made by the boat's speed
The current is dragging the air along
A sea breeze is starting to blow
The instrument needs calibrating
questions.why: Moving through still air at 6 kn makes a 6 kn apparent wind from ahead.

questions.q: On this course the genoa keeps collapsing and flapping. Why?
options: The wind is too strong for a genoa
The mainsail is blocking its wind
The boat is in the no-go zone
The genoa halyard is too tight
questions.why: Dead downwind the main shades the genoa; goose-wing it or come up a little.

questions.q: How does the boat get to the harbour under sail?
options: It cannot: yachts only sail across the wind
By gybing back and forth downwind
By tacking: close-hauled on one tack, then the other
Straight at it, with both sheets eased
questions.why: No boat sails inside the no-go zone, so you zigzag upwind close-hauled.

questions.q: What does the skipper want you to do with the mainsheet?
options: Keep it cleated so the boat stays steady
Pull in harder in each gust for more power
Ease it right out and leave it there
Ease in each gust, pull back in as it passes
questions.why: Easing in a gust spills wind and cuts the heel; sheeting back in keeps the drive.

questions.q: What happens to the wind you feel on board?

figure.title: Bearing away
lines: From close-hauled to a broad reach
Boat speed rises from 6 to 7 kn

options: It gets lighter and comes from further aft
It gets stronger and comes from further forward
It gets lighter and comes from further forward
It stays the same: only the true wind counts
questions.why: Upwind the boat's speed adds to the wind you feel; downwind it subtracts, and the wind moves aft.

questions.q: The helm gybes onto starboard tack. Which genoa sheet takes the load afterwards?

figure.note: Run on port tack, genoa out to starboard

options: The starboard sheet: it stays the working one
The port sheet: the sails are now to port
Both sheets equally until the next tack
Neither: the genoa is furled for every gybe
questions.why: In a gybe the sails cross to the other side, so the other sheet becomes the working sheet.

questions.q: You are trimming the sails. Which wind do they actually feel?
options: The true wind, at about 90°
A mix of both, at about 75°
The apparent wind, at about 60°
Whichever is stronger at the time
questions.why: Sails feel the wind on the moving boat: the apparent wind, forward of the true wind.

questions.q: During a tack, the crew on the old genoa sheet lets it go the moment "Ready about" is called, before the boat starts to turn. What is the result?
options: The boat turns faster with less load on the sail
Nothing: the timing of the release makes no difference
The genoa backs and pushes the bow through the wind
The genoa flaps, the boat loses speed and may stall head to wind
questions.why: Released early, the genoa stops driving and the boat may stop in irons; let go as the bow passes the wind.

questions.q: The skipper wants a loop in the end of a line that a swimmer can slip over their head and under their arms. It must not tighten. Which knot?
options: Bowline
Clove hitch
Reef knot
Rolling hitch
questions.why: A bowline makes a fixed loop that does not slip or tighten under load.

questions.q: The mainsheet runs through several blocks to the cockpit. What do you tie in its tail so it can never run out through them?
options: Sheet bend
Figure-of-eight
Clove hitch
Bowline
questions.why: A figure-of-eight is the stopper knot: too fat to pass through a block.

questions.q: The lazy-bag zip has broken, so you tie the furled main to the boom with sail ties. Which knot?
options: Clove hitch
Sheet bend
Reef knot
Rolling hitch
questions.why: Tying round a bundle is the reef knot's job: it lies flat and unties easily.

questions.q: You are on fender duty, and the skipper will want the fenders raised or lowered as you come in. What do you tie them on with?
options: Reef knot
Sheet bend
Bowline
Clove hitch
questions.why: A clove hitch is quick to tie and easy to slide up or down to change the height.

questions.q: The tender's painter is too short to reach the ring on the quay, and the only spare is a thinner line. Which knot joins them?
options: Sheet bend
Reef knot
Clove hitch
Figure-of-eight
questions.why: A sheet bend joins two lines and holds even when they are different thicknesses.

questions.q: The snubber must grip the chain when it is pulled along it. Which knot do you tie?

figure.title: At anchor on all chain
lines: Snubber line ready on the foredeck
Skipper: "Tie it on to the chain"

options: Clove hitch
Rolling hitch
Reef knot
Bowline
questions.why: A rolling hitch grips a rope, spar or chain against a pull along its length.

questions.q: You tied this fender on with a clove hitch. How do you stop it slipping?

figure.note: The fender slips lower each time the boat rolls

options: Tie a figure-of-eight at the fender end
Wet the line so it grips the rail
Add a half hitch round the standing part
Re-tie it as a sheet bend
questions.why: A half hitch round the standing part locks a clove hitch that works loose.

questions.q: You leave the tender on this ring while you have dinner ashore. Which knot will not shake loose as the tender jerks all evening?

figure.note: Wash from passing boats all evening

options: Clove hitch
Sheet bend
Reef knot
Round turn and two half hitches
questions.why: The round turn takes the jerks and the two half hitches stay put.

questions.q: You are making the stern line fast on this cleat. What does the line do first?
options: A full turn round the base of the cleat
A figure-of-eight over the horns
A bowline round one of the horns
A locking hitch over one horn
questions.why: The turn round the base takes the load; then figure-eights and one locking hitch.

questions.q: A new crew member finishes a cleat hitch with three locking hitches piled on top. Why does the skipper ask for it to be re-tied?
options: It makes the line too short to reach
It can jam and is slow to free in a hurry
Three hitches can slip off under load
It wears out the cleat's horns faster
questions.why: One locking hitch holds; more can jam just when you need to let the line go fast.

questions.q: You have coiled a mooring line and want to hang it in the locker without it coming undone. How do you finish the coil?
options: Tie the two free ends together with a reef knot
Wind the coil tightly round your hand and elbow first
Wrap the end round the coil, pass a loop through and over the top
Tuck the loose end in among the loops of the coil
questions.why: Turns round the coil and a loop over the top hold it neat, and it is quick to free.

questions.q: You are about to throw the stern line to a marinero on the quay. What do you do with the boat's end of the line?
options: Tie it to the guardrail with a clove hitch
Hold it in your other hand as you throw
Leave it loose on deck so it can pay out
Make it fast on the stern cleat first
questions.why: If the boat's end is not made fast, a good throw can send the whole line ashore or into the sea.

questions.q: How do you hold the coiled line to throw it ashore?
options: Split the coil: throw one half, let the rest run from your hand
Throw the whole coil in one bundle, as hard as you can
Throw the loose end first, then the whole coil after it
Wrap the coil round your hand and throw it as one
questions.why: Half the coil carries the line; the rest runs out freely from your open hand without tangling.

questions.q: You cannot hold the boat by hand. What do you do?

figure.title: Med mooring, crosswind
lines: You are on the quay with a stern line
A gust pushes the boat sideways
The line goes bar-tight in your hands

options: Loop it round your waist and lean back
Take a turn round a bollard and hold the tail
Wrap the line round your hand for grip
Brace your feet and pull harder
questions.why: A turn round a bollard takes the load; a line wrapped round you can drag you in.

questions.q: Ashore, you tie a mooring line to a post with a round turn and two half hitches while the wind pulls the boat away. Why take the round turn first?
options: It lets the knot slip off in a hurry
It locks the hitches so they never undo
It holds the strain while you tie the hitches
It makes the line shorter and neater
questions.why: The friction of the full turn holds the load, so the half hitches are tied in slack line.

questions.q: You have just left the marina and the mooring lines lie in a heap in the cockpit. What do you do?
options: Throw them down below into the saloon
Hang them over the guardrail to dry
Leave them out, ready for tonight's berth
Coil and stow them so none can trail over the side
questions.why: A loose line can slip over the side and wrap round the propeller, or trip someone.

questions.q: You have these three jobs to do. Which knots do you tie, in order?

figure.title: Three jobs
lines: 1. Join two lines of different thickness
2. Hang a fender on the guardrail
3. A fixed loop to drop over a bollard

options: Sheet bend, clove hitch, bowline
Reef knot, clove hitch, bowline
Reef knot, rolling hitch, bowline
Sheet bend, bowline, clove hitch
questions.why: A sheet bend joins unequal lines, a clove hitch hangs fenders, a bowline makes a fixed loop.

questions.q: You are about to throw the stern line. Where do you aim?

figure.title: Throwing a line ashore
lines: Strong wind blowing from your left
Marinero on the quay, 4 m away
Line coiled, boat's end made fast

options: Straight at the marinero's chest
A little to the left of the marinero, upwind
High over the marinero's head
A little to the right of the marinero, downwind
questions.why: The wind carries the line sideways as it flies, so aim upwind of your target.

questions.q: The line on this cleat is heavily loaded. How do you let out a metre safely?

figure.note: Skipper: "Ease the bow line a metre"

options: Throw off every turn at once and let the line run out
Wrap the tail round your hand for grip, then uncleat it
Take off the hitch and figure-eights, keep a turn, ease round
Untie it completely and tie a fresh bowline further along
questions.why: A turn round the base keeps control while you surge the line out against the friction.

questions.q: You are on the stern line as the boat reverses in. What do you do now?

figure.title: Stern-to, reversing in
lines: Your stern line fell short, into the sea
It is sinking close to the stern

options: Ask the marinero to fish it out
Leave it there and throw a second line
Throw the rest of the coil after it
Warn the helm and haul the line in fast
questions.why: A line in the water by the stern can wrap round the propeller: the helm must know, and it must come out fast.

questions.q: You are putting the genoa sheet on this winch. Which way do the turns go round the drum?
options: Clockwise
Clockwise to port, anticlockwise to starboard
Either way: the drum turns both ways
Anticlockwise
questions.why: Yacht winches turn clockwise only, so the sheet goes on clockwise.

questions.q: You have finished winding in the genoa sheet. What do you do with the winch handle?
options: Lay it on the cockpit seat nearby
Take it out and put it in its pocket
Leave it in, turned to point aft
Leave it in the winch for next time
questions.why: A handle left in the winch fouls sheets and people, and is easily knocked overboard.

questions.q: You have motored out of the harbour and the sails are going up. What do you do with the fenders?
options: Lower them to touch the water
Leave them out for the next harbour
Take them in and stow them
Tie them up higher on the guardrail
questions.why: Fenders hanging at sea bang the hull and get lost; bring them in once clear of the harbour.

questions.q: Coming alongside, you stand by with the bow line coiled. When do you get off onto the pontoon?
options: When the bow first touches the pontoon
As soon as you can jump the gap
Before the boat slows, to save time
When the boat is close and nearly stopped, by stepping
questions.why: Step, never jump: a jump can end between the boat and the pontoon.

questions.q: A crew member is winding the winch and you are tailing. What is your job?
options: Keep steady tension on the tail as it comes off
Push the turns down the drum with your hand
Let go of the tail whenever they pause
Hold the tail loosely so it can slip
questions.why: Without tension on the tail the sheet slips on the drum and the winding is wasted.

questions.q: This winch is a self-tailer. How do you load the sheet so you can wind with both hands?
options: Straight into the jaws with no turns
A few turns clockwise, then into the jaws on top
One turn anticlockwise, then into the jaws
Turns clockwise, then cleat the tail below
questions.why: The turns grip the drum; the jaws on top hold the tail, so no one needs to tail.

questions.q: Winding in the genoa sheet, you see this, and the sheet will neither come in nor ease. What do you do?
options: Keep winding: it will free itself
Pull the crossed turns off by hand
Stop, keep your hands clear and call the skipper
Take the handle out and spin the drum back
questions.why: A riding turn locks a loaded sheet; fingers near the drum can be trapped.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to ease the loaded genoa sheet a little. How do you do it?
options: Take all the turns off and hold the tail
Wind the winch handle backwards
Wrap the tail once round your hand for grip
Ease the tail out slowly, fingers clear of the turns
questions.why: A loaded sheet can jerk, and fingers near the drum get pulled into the turns.

questions.q: You are getting the fenders ready for tonight's berth. Where do you hang them?

figure.title: Stern-to tonight
lines: Yachts already berthed on both sides
Quay about 1 m above the water

options: Both sides, at the widest part, level with the neighbours
At the bow only, to protect the anchor and pulpit
One side only, the side the wind is coming from
At the stern only, hanging low down by the water
questions.why: Stern-to, your sides lie against the yachts next to you, so the fenders go on both sides.

questions.q: The skipper points at your fenders as you come in. What do you change?

figure.title: Coming alongside
lines: Your fenders hang at deck level

options: Nothing: at deck level they guard the rail
Lower them to where the pontoon will touch the hull
Take them in: a pontoon is soft
Raise them higher, to the top of the rail
questions.why: Fenders hang where the hull meets the pontoon edge, here close to the water.

questions.q: Alongside, the skipper asks you to rig a spring from the bow cleat. Where does it lead ashore?
options: Forward along the quay, ahead of the bow
Straight across, to the nearest bollard
Aft along the quay, to a bollard near the stern
Back to the boat's own stern cleat
questions.why: A spring runs diagonally: from the bow it leads aft, from the stern it leads forward.

questions.q: Med mooring, you have walked the lazy line up to the bow cleat. What do you do before making it fast?
options: Pass it back to the marinero to hold
Leave some slack so the boat can swing
Cleat it slack: it is only a back-up
Haul it in hard until it is taut, then cleat it
questions.why: The lazy line does the anchor's job: pulled taut, it holds the bow off and the stern clear of the quay.

questions.q: You are at the stern as the boat backs in. What do you do?

figure.title: Stern-to, the last metre
lines: The stern swings towards the quay corner
No fender hangs at that spot
You are standing at the stern

options: Put a loose fender in the gap and keep your hands out
Jump onto the quay and push the boat off
Push the boat off the quay with your foot
Hold the stern off with both hands
questions.why: Never put hands or feet between boat and quay: tonnes of boat will crush them.

questions.q: The tender is towed astern on a long painter, and the skipper is about to reverse into a berth. What do you do with the painter?
options: Let it out longer so the tender trails clear
Shorten it or bring the tender alongside, clear of the prop
Leave it: going astern, the tender drifts away
Hand it to the helm to hold while reversing
questions.why: Going astern the boat runs over a slack painter, and it can wrap round the propeller.

questions.q: Before leaving, the skipper asks you to rig the stern line as a slip line, so you can let it go from on board. What do you do?
options: Tie a bowline round the bollard instead of a hitch
Make it fast with two cleat hitches on the boat's cleat
Lead it round the bollard and back, both ends cleated aboard
Tie a second line to the same bollard as a back-up
questions.why: With both ends aboard, you let one end go and pull the line back round the bollard.

questions.q: The tender is alongside and the crew are climbing down into it. When do you untie the painter?
options: When the first person is in
First, so it is ready to go
Before boarding, then hold it by hand
Last, when everyone is in and seated
questions.why: While the painter is tied on, the tender cannot drift off as people climb in.

questions.q: You are helping the skipper clear a riding turn. What is the next step?

figure.title: Riding turn
lines: Genoa sheet jammed on the winch
Spare line tied on with a rolling hitch
Spare line led to the other winch

options: Winch in the spare line, then clear the slack turns
Untie the spare line now it has gripped
Wind the jammed winch harder to free it
Cut the jammed sheet, as it is backed up
questions.why: The spare line takes the load; only an unloaded sheet can be unwound safely.

questions.q: The wind pushes the boat along the quay. Which lines take the strain?

figure.title: Alongside, starboard side-to
lines: The boat is pushed forward along the quay
Lines: bow, stern and two springs

options: The bow line and the spring led forward from the stern
The stern line and the spring led aft from the bow
Only the bow line, as the boat moves forward
All four lines share the load equally
questions.why: Lines leading aft from the boat stop it moving forward: the stern line and the spring from the bow.

questions.q: Coming alongside, you are to step ashore with a line. Where on deck do you step off from?
options: From the coachroof, for extra height
Right at the bow, as it arrives first
By the shrouds, where the boat is widest and closest
From the bathing platform at the stern
questions.why: At the shrouds the boat is widest and steadiest, and there is something to hold as you step.

questions.q: Which stern line do you pass ashore first?

figure.title: Reversing stern-to
lines: Two stern lines ready, one each side

options: Both together, one in each hand
The starboard one, on the leeward side
Whichever is nearer the marinero
The port one, on the windward side
questions.why: The windward line stops the stern blowing downwind onto the neighbours.

questions.q: You are steering with a tiller and want the bow to turn to port. Which way do you move the tiller?
options: To starboard
Hold it central and wait
To port
Straight back towards you
questions.why: A tiller works the opposite way: push it to starboard and the bow swings to port.

questions.q: You are steering with a wheel and want to turn to starboard. Which way do you turn it?
options: Anticlockwise, then back to the centre
Clockwise, like a car
Either way: the rudder finds the course
Anticlockwise, the opposite way
questions.why: A wheel steers like a car: turn it to starboard to go to starboard.

questions.q: You call "Ready about" and the crew answer "Ready". What do you call as you put the helm over?
options: "Ready about!" again
"Let go!"
"Lee-oh!"
"Gybe-oh!"
questions.why: "Lee-oh" (or "Helm's a-lee") tells the crew the bow is now turning through the wind.

questions.q: The engine is off, there is no wind and the boat is drifting. You turn the wheel but the bow does not answer. Why?
options: The wheel needs turning much faster
The wheel has come off the rudder
The rudder only works under engine
No water is flowing past the rudder
questions.why: A rudder steers only when water flows over it: no way on, no steering.

questions.q: You have just taken the wheel. Which way do you turn?
options: To starboard, about 10°
To starboard, about 140°
Neither: the compass will catch up
To port, about 10°
questions.why: Headings grow clockwise: to go from 130° to 140°, turn 10° to starboard.

questions.q: The skipper gives you 090° towards a headland 8 miles away. The compass swings in the waves and is tiring to watch. What helps?
options: Chase every swing of the compass card
Steer for a landmark on 090° and check the compass now and then
Steer by the wake astern and ignore the compass
Steer for the nearest boat on that side
questions.why: A fixed landmark is steadier to steer for; the compass confirms you are still on course.

questions.q: You are steering and see this on the genoa. What do you do with the helm?
options: Luff up a little until both stream
Tack at once onto the other tack
Bear away a little until both stream
Hold this heading: all is well
questions.why: A lifting windward tell-tale means you are too close to the wind: bear away.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to sail as close to the wind as you can. How do you find the limit?
options: Head up until the boat stops, then hold that heading
Steer straight into the wind and wait
Bear away until the boat heels hard, then hold it
Head up slowly until the genoa luff lifts, then bear away a touch
questions.why: The edge of the no-go zone is where the luff starts to lift; just below it the sails drive.

questions.q: On a run, the skipper asks you to gybe. What do you call, and when?
options: "Ready to gybe", wait for "Ready", then "Gybe-oh" as you turn
"Ready to gybe", then turn without waiting
"Ready about", wait for "Ready", then "Lee-oh"
"Gybe-oh", turn at once, then "Ready to gybe"
questions.why: Warn, wait for every crew member to answer, then call as the stern goes through the wind.

questions.q: You are helming into a crowded marina under engine. What speed do you keep?
options: Whatever the skipper set out at sea
Slow, but enough to keep steering
Brisk, for good control in the wind
None: engine in neutral, drifting in
questions.why: Go no faster than you would be happy to hit something at, but keep enough way to steer.

questions.q: Motoring slowly astern, you want the stern to swing to starboard. Which way do you turn the wheel?
options: Amidships: going astern you cannot steer
To port, then give a burst ahead
To starboard: astern, the stern follows the wheel
To port: astern, the steering is reversed
questions.why: Going astern with a wheel, turn it the way you want the stern to go.

questions.q: You are at the wheel and put the engine into reverse. What do you expect first?
options: The stern swings to starboard at first
Nothing until you turn the wheel
The bow swings to port at first
The stern swings to port before she gathers way
questions.why: Prop walk pushes the stern sideways in reverse, most of all before the boat is moving.

questions.q: Two crew are working at the mast, sorting out a halyard. You are on the helm. What do you do?
options: Hold a steady course and warn them before any turn
Leave the helm for a moment to help them
Steer for the smoothest water, turning often
Speed up so they are finished sooner
questions.why: Sudden turns or heel throw crew on deck off balance; keep her steady and call any change.

questions.q: Under engine, the skipper asks you to hold the boat head to wind while the crew hoist the main. How do you know you are head to wind?
options: The genoa sheet goes tight
The masthead wind arrow points dead ahead
The boom swings out to one side
The wind is on the back of your neck
questions.why: Head to wind, the wind comes over the bow, so the masthead arrow points straight forward.

questions.q: On your first spell at the wheel, the boat wanders 20° either side of the course. What helps most?
options: Big turns of the wheel to get back quickly
Holding the wheel rigid, never moving it
Small, early corrections, then wait for her to answer
Steering by the compass only, never ahead
questions.why: A boat answers the helm slowly; small early corrections stop you over-steering.

questions.q: You call "Ready about". One crew answers "Ready", but the one on the other sheet is still putting turns on the winch. What do you do?
options: Call "Lee-oh" louder and start the turn
Tack, and let them catch up after
Tack anyway: one crew member is enough
Wait until everyone has answered "Ready"
questions.why: Only start the turn when every crew member has answered "Ready".

questions.q: A wave pushes the stern on this course. Which turn of the bow risks an accidental gybe?
options: A turn to starboard, towards the boom
Any turn at all, either way
A turn to port, away from the boom
None: on a run the boom cannot cross
questions.why: Turning towards the boom side takes the stern through the wind, and the boom slams across.

questions.q: You are steering with a tiller from the windward side. The skipper says "Bear away a little". Which way do you move the tiller?
options: It depends which tack you are on
Towards you, to windward
Hold it central: the sheets steer
Away from you, towards the boom
questions.why: Tiller to windward turns the bow to leeward, away from the wind: that is bearing away.

questions.q: The skipper beside you asks what you would do. What is the best answer?

figure.title: Entering the marina
lines: The bow is blowing off sideways

options: A long burst astern to stop the boat
Engine to neutral, and wait for the wind to drop
A short burst ahead, to push water over the rudder
Turn the wheel hard over the other way
questions.why: Too slow, the rudder has no grip; a burst of propeller wash over it brings the steering back.

questions.q: Anna is taking over the helm from you. What do you tell her?
options: How long you steered, and the boat speed
Only the course: she can see the rest
Only the ferry: the course can wait
The course, the wind, and the ferry ahead
questions.why: A handover gives the course, the wind and sail trim, and any traffic to watch.

questions.q: You arrive late on the first evening and miss the skipper's safety briefing. What do you do before the boat leaves?
options: Ask the skipper to walk you through it
Ask another guest to sum it up on your watch
Nothing — you will pick it up as you go
Read the boat's manual once you are under way
questions.why: You must know where the safety gear is before you sail, and only the skipper's briefing covers this boat.

questions.q: You are packing for a week's charter from Lefkada. Which shoes do you take for deck work?
options: Flip-flops that dry quickly
Deck shoes with non-slip, non-marking soles
Black-soled trainers with a deep tread
Leather shoes with smooth soles
questions.why: Soft non-slip soles grip a wet deck and leave no black marks; flip-flops come off your feet.

questions.q: You must carry two fenders forward along the side deck while the boat rolls in a ferry's wake. How do you do it?
options: Both at once, walking quickly forward
One at a time, steadying yourself on the boom
One at a time, holding on with your free hand
Both at once, hugged to your chest
questions.why: One hand for yourself, one for the boat — and the boom is no handhold, it swings.

questions.q: What do you do to stay fit for your watches today?

figure.title: Passage day, August
lines: Air 35 °C, little shade in the cockpit

options: Drink only once you feel really thirsty
Save the water until the end of the day
Swap water for cold beer — it is still fluid
Drink water often, before you feel thirsty
questions.why: In heat you lose water all the time; thirst comes late, and alcohol dries you out further.

questions.q: This is what you find on your lifejacket. What do you do?
options: Hand it to the skipper and take another one
Wear it — red shows it is ready to fire
Blow it up by mouth to test, then wear it
Wear it and rely on the oral tube instead
questions.why: A red indicator means the inflator may not fire; the jacket must be re-armed before use.

questions.q: A wave fills the cockpit and your automatic lifejacket inflates. Later you let the air out. Can you wear it on your next watch?
options: Yes — a spare charge fires next time
No — it needs a re-arming kit fitted first
Yes, once it has dried in the sun
Yes — just let the air out and fold it
questions.why: A fired jacket has an empty cylinder; it will not inflate again until it is re-armed.

questions.q: Your friend finds her lifejacket's crotch strap uncomfortable and leaves it undone. What happens if she goes over the side?
options: Nothing — the waist belt alone holds it in place
The jacket will not inflate on contact with water
The jacket rides up over her face as it inflates
The cylinder fires early as she moves about
questions.why: Without the crotch strap an inflated jacket slides up and can cover the face or come off.

questions.q: Your skipper says lifejackets go on whenever there is a real risk of ending up in the water. In which of these do you wear yours?
options: Hosing down the deck while tied up in the marina
Sitting in the cockpit while moored stern-to in harbour
Sleeping in your bunk during your off watch
The tender ride back to the boat after dinner ashore
questions.why: Night tender trips, often after a drink, are a classic way to drown — wear a lifejacket.

questions.q: The skipper sends you forward to free a jammed furling line. Which side deck do you use?
options: Port — the high, windward side
Starboard — the low, leeward side
Either — the heel makes no difference
Starboard, holding the boom as you go
questions.why: On the windward side a slip throws you onto the deck, not over the low guardrail.

questions.q: You need to cross the cockpit to reach the cool box. What is the main danger to you?

figure.title: Downwind run
lines: Wind F4 from astern, following sea
Boat rolling, main out to starboard

options: The genoa backing and stopping the boat
An accidental gybe swinging the boom across
The boat suddenly luffing head to wind
The mainsheet jamming in its block
questions.why: Running in a rolling sea, the boom can gybe without warning at head height — keep low.

questions.q: You check this list after the skipper's briefing. What is still missing from it?

figure.title: Briefing — what you were shown
lines: Flares and liferaft: cockpit and stern

options: Where the spare bedding and towels are kept
Which marina the boat will use tonight
Where the first-aid kit and the bilge pump are
How the plotter's tide page works
questions.why: A safety briefing covers the first-aid kit and the bilge pump too — ask if they were missed.

questions.q: You are on deck all day in July with a cool breeze blowing. How do you protect yourself from the sun?
options: Cover up only at the first sign of redness
No cover needed — the breeze stops sunburn
Sunscreen once in the morning is enough
Hat, long sleeves, sunglasses, sunscreen topped up
questions.why: Wind cools the skin but does not stop UV; the sun and its glare off the water burn all day.

questions.q: You are helming at night as the wind rises, and the skipper tells you to clip on. Where do you clip your tether?
options: A strong point in the cockpit meant for it
The guardwire beside the wheel
The mainsheet traveller car
A stanchion next to the helm
questions.why: Use a proper strong point: guardwires and stanchions can fail and the traveller car moves.

questions.q: Your tether has two hooks. Clipped to the jackstay, you reach the mast and must move to the strong point there. How?
options: Unclip and hold the mast — it is only a minute
Clip the second hook on, then unclip the first
Unclip from the jackstay, then clip to the mast
Hold a shroud while you move the one hook
questions.why: With two hooks you are never unclipped: always clip on before you unclip.

questions.q: Rain starts and you put on your foul-weather jacket. Where does your lifejacket go?
options: Under the jacket, to keep it dry
Under the jacket, so it cannot snag on lines
Over the jacket, so it can inflate freely
Either way — it inflates the same
questions.why: Under a jacket it cannot inflate properly and squeezes your chest; wear it on top.

questions.q: The skipper's standing order is 'clip on at night'. You come up for your 22:00 watch on a calm, starry night. What do you do?
options: Clip on only if you go forward of the mast
Skip it — the moon gives enough light
Skip it — the rule is meant for rough weather
Clip on before you step out of the companionway
questions.why: A night rule has no exceptions: someone who falls over in the dark is very hard to find.

questions.q: What do you do before you leave the cockpit?

figure.title: Reefing at night
lines: Skipper needs you at the mast
Spray over the deck, boat heeling

options: Lifejacket fastened, clip on, tell the helmsman
Harness on; no lifejacket needed when clipped
Lifejacket on; clip on only if it gets worse
Lifejacket on, clip on once you reach the mast
questions.why: Clip on in the cockpit before you move, and let the helm know you are going forward.

questions.q: You want to go forward and secure the halyard. What do you do first?

figure.title: Alone on watch
lines: A halyard has come loose at the mast

options: Go once the deck lights are switched on
Wake another crew member before you go
Go quickly unclipped, wearing your lifejacket
Go forward clipped on, without waking anyone
questions.why: Never leave the cockpit alone at night: if you fell in, nobody would know you were gone.

questions.q: At night, in a moderate sea, your friend is seasick and needs to be sick over the side. What do you do?
options: Take her to the windward rail, the high side
Let her use the leeward rail, unclipped
Take her to the leeward rail, clipped on, and stay
Let her go to the leeward rail alone, for privacy
questions.why: Be sick to leeward so it blows away — but clipped on and watched: that is the rail people fall over.

questions.q: What do you advise your cousin?

figure.title: A guest aboard
lines: Calm and sunny, motoring along the coast

options: Put one on only once the wind gets up
None needed in calm water in daylight
None needed if she stays in the cockpit
Wear a lifejacket on deck whenever under way
questions.why: A non-swimmer wears a lifejacket on deck at all times under way, whatever the weather.

questions.q: You are the lookout on this yacht. Where is your blind spot?
options: On the port bow, behind the genoa
Straight ahead, behind the mast
Abeam to starboard, by the shrouds
On the starboard bow, to windward
questions.why: The genoa hides the leeward bow — on starboard tack that is to port, so look under it often.

questions.q: You are motoring at 6 knots and keeping a careful watch ahead. How often do you look astern?
options: Only at night, when lights show up
Regularly — fast boats come up from behind
Only when the skipper asks you to
Never — an overtaking boat must keep clear
questions.why: A lookout covers all round; fast ferries and RIBs overtake quickly and quietly.

questions.q: You spot this ship. How do you report it to the skipper?
options: 'Ship at twelve o'clock, about two miles'
'Ship at nine o'clock, about two miles'
'Ship at three o'clock, about two miles'
'Ship at six o'clock, about two miles'
questions.why: Clock bearings count from your own bow: 12 is dead ahead, 3 is abeam to starboard.

questions.q: You have been taking bearings of this ship. What do you tell the skipper?
options: Risk only once the bearing starts to change
No risk while it is more than a mile away
No risk — the ship is holding a steady course
Bearing steady and closing — risk of collision
questions.why: A steady bearing on a vessel that is getting closer means you are on a collision course.

questions.q: You check a yacht three times with the compass. What do you report?
options: Bearing changing — it should pass clear, keep watching
It will hit us — the helm must tack at once
Bearing steady — there is a risk of collision
Bearings tell you nothing about the risk
questions.why: A clearly changing bearing usually means you will pass clear — but keep checking until it is past.

questions.q: You are sailing towards this boat. Who keeps clear?
options: The trawler — power gives way to sail
You do — a boat fishing comes first
Neither — both turn to starboard
The smaller of the two boats
questions.why: Rule 18: a sailing vessel keeps out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing.

questions.q: You see these lights. Which way is the vessel heading?
options: Crossing ahead of you from left to right
Coming straight towards you
Crossing ahead of you from right to left
Moving directly away from you
questions.why: You see its red port side, so its bow points to your left; the white light shows it is under power.

questions.q: At night you are motoring up behind a slower yacht to overtake it. What do you see of its lights?
options: A green light only
A red and a green light side by side
A white light above a red one
A single white light only
questions.why: From astern you see only the white sternlight; the sidelights are hidden from behind.

questions.q: You see only these two lights, close together at masthead height. What are they?

figure.note: Night · almost dead ahead, high up

options: A sailing yacht heading towards you
A fishing boat working its nets
A yacht lying at anchor for the night
A motor boat heading away from you
questions.why: A masthead tricolour: red and green together mean a sailing boat is bows-on to you.

questions.q: A motor boat ahead of you gives one short blast on its horn. What is it telling you?
options: 'I doubt that you are keeping clear'
'I am altering my course to starboard'
'I am operating astern propulsion'
'I am altering my course to port'
questions.why: Rule 34: one short blast — altering to starboard; two — to port; three — going astern.

questions.q: You are sailing across a ferry route, holding your course. The approaching ferry sounds five short, rapid blasts. What does it mean, and what do you do?
options: It is going astern — carry on as you are
It is giving way to you — carry on as you are
It doubts your intentions — tell the skipper now
It is turning to port — carry on as you are
questions.why: Rule 34(d): five or more short blasts signal doubt or a warning — act at once.

questions.q: In the harbour, a large motor yacht leaving the quay sounds three short blasts. What is it doing?
options: It is turning to starboard
It is turning to port
It doubts what you are doing
Its engines are going astern
questions.why: Rule 34: three short blasts mean 'I am operating astern propulsion'.

questions.q: This motor boat is closing on a steady bearing. Who should keep clear?
options: Usually the motor boat — power gives way to sail
Whichever boat is going faster
You — a boat on your starboard side has priority
Neither — both boats turn to port
questions.why: Rule 18: a power-driven vessel keeps out of the way of a sailing vessel, with a few exceptions.

questions.q: You are sailing faster than a yacht ahead on the same course and slowly catching it up. Who keeps clear?
options: Whichever boat is on port tack
You — the overtaking boat keeps clear
The yacht ahead — it must let you pass
The yacht with the bigger sails
questions.why: Rule 13: an overtaking vessel keeps clear, whatever its type or tack.

questions.q: You are motoring and this boat is coming straight at you. What should happen?
options: Both boats turn to port
The smaller boat stops
Both boats turn to starboard
You hold course; it turns
questions.why: Rule 14: head-on under power, each turns to starboard and they pass port to port.

questions.q: Your friend says the ferry must give way because you are sailing. What do you say?

figure.title: Harbour entrance
lines: Big ferry leaving the narrow entrance
Little room for it to turn
You are under sail, about to cross its bow

options: Stop in the entrance and let it go round
Right — power always gives way to sail
Cross quickly ahead before it speeds up
No — in a narrow entrance we keep clear of it
questions.why: Rule 9: a sailing yacht must not impede a big ship that can only use a narrow channel.

questions.q: You are on night watch and need to check something on the chart. Which light do you use?
options: A dim red light
A bright white torch, briefly
Your phone screen on full brightness
The saloon lights, switched on fully
questions.why: Red light keeps your night vision; white light can spoil it for many minutes.

questions.q: You are watching this vessel at night. What has it done?

figure.title: Night watch
lines: 21:10 — a white light above a green one
21:15 — a red light appears by the green

options: Switched its engine off and set sail
Turned towards you — it now heads straight at you
Stopped and dropped anchor for the night
Turned away from you — it is now moving off
questions.why: Seeing both sidelights means its bow points at you — report it to the skipper at once.

questions.q: You see this group of lights. What do you tell the skipper?
options: A large ship moving away from you
Two small boats, one behind the other
A large ship crossing from right to left
A sailing yacht heading towards you
questions.why: Two masthead lights mean a ship over 50 m; the lower one is forward, and red is its port side.

questions.q: As lookout, how do you handle this motor boat?

figure.title: Your watch, 14:00
lines: Motor boat on the port bow
You are under sail, skipper below

options: Steer away yourself without telling anyone
Say nothing — power gives way to sail
Wait until it is close enough to be sure
Call the skipper now, with bearing and distance
questions.why: Report early: a steady bearing means risk of collision, and the skipper needs time to decide.

questions.q: The morning forecast says 'northerly, Force 5'. Which way is the wind blowing?
options: From the north, towards the south
From the south, towards the north
From the west, turning north later
From the sea, towards the north
questions.why: Wind is always named by the direction it blows from.

questions.q: The forecast for your day sail is Force 4. What kind of day is that for a yacht?
options: A gale, 34–40 knots — stay in harbour
A moderate breeze, 11–16 knots — good sailing
A strong breeze, 22–27 knots — reefs needed
Near calm — expect to motor most of the day
questions.why: Force 4 is a moderate breeze, 11–16 knots, small waves with some white horses.

questions.q: The afternoon forecast is north-west Force 6, and your crossing is 18 miles of open water. What does this mean for you as crew?
options: Moderate breeze — full sail and a gentle ride
Storm force — no yacht could put to sea
Strong wind — expect reefs, spray and a lively ride
Light airs — expect to motor most of the way
questions.why: Force 6 is a strong breeze, 22–27 knots: reefs, rough water and lifejackets on.

questions.q: The skipper decides to stay in port because the forecast is Force 8. What does that mean?
options: A moderate breeze, about 11–16 knots
A light breeze, about 4–6 knots
A fresh breeze, about 17–21 knots
A gale, about 34–40 knots
questions.why: Force 8 is a gale — too much for a charter yacht and her crew.

questions.q: What wind do you expect by mid-afternoon?

figure.title: Hot summer day, Saronic Gulf
lines: The land is heating up fast

options: A breeze blowing in from the sea onto the land
Flat calm until sunset
A wind that dies away by noon
A breeze blowing off the land out to sea
questions.why: Land heats faster than sea; the air over it rises and a sea breeze blows in by the afternoon.

questions.q: You are on anchor watch at 02:00 in a calm bay below hills. A light breeze springs up. Where does it most likely come from?
options: Off the sea, blowing onto the land
Off the land, blowing out to sea
Along the shore, from the east
Any side — night winds are random
questions.why: At night the land cools faster than the sea, so a light land breeze blows offshore.

questions.q: You are sailing in the Cyclades in August. From which direction does the Meltemi usually blow?
options: From the south, strongest at night
From the west, only after rain
From the north, strongest in the afternoon
From the east, only in early spring
questions.why: The Meltemi is the Aegean's summer north wind, usually at its strongest in the afternoon.

questions.q: Your next hop is 20 miles north across open water, and the Meltemi is forecast at Force 6–7 for three days. When is the crossing likely to be easiest?
options: Leave mid-afternoon, after lunch
Leave at noon, when it is warm
Any time — the Meltemi is steady
Leave early, around dawn
questions.why: The Meltemi often eases overnight and builds through the day — cross early.

questions.q: Close under the cliffs the water looks calm. What do you expect there?
options: Sudden strong gusts falling off the cliffs
A steady light breeze — it is sheltered
A steady wind, just like offshore
Flat calm — a safe place to drift
questions.why: Wind spilling over high land drops down the lee side in violent gusts.

questions.q: You are about to sail through the gap at A. What do you expect?
options: The wind swinging round to the south
Stronger wind, squeezed through the gap
Lighter wind, sheltered by both islands
No change from the open sea
questions.why: Wind funnels between islands and round headlands — expect it to be stronger there.

questions.q: You are keeping the barometer log. What do you tell the skipper?
options: It is steady — settled weather ahead
It is rising — the wind should ease
It is falling fast — strong wind may be on the way
Pressure means little in summer
questions.why: A fall of several hPa in three hours is a warning that strong wind is coming.

questions.q: What is most likely on the way?

figure.title: Afternoon, near the coast
lines: Hot and sticky since the morning
Tall cauliflower clouds over the hills
Tops spreading out flat, like an anvil

options: A long spell of settled calm weather
A steady sea breeze, slowly building
Fog rolling in from the open sea
A thunderstorm with sudden violent gusts
questions.why: Towering clouds with anvil tops are thunderstorm clouds: squalls, lightning and heavy rain.

questions.q: The skipper asks what to get ready. What do you suggest?

figure.title: Squall line ahead
lines: Dark wall of cloud, rain below it
Dark ruffled water coming your way

options: Reduce sail now and put lifejackets on
Keep full sail and try to outrun it
Wait for the first gust, then reef
Go below and leave the sails as they are
questions.why: Reef before a squall arrives — its first gust can be far stronger than the wind ahead of it.

questions.q: What does the visibility part of this forecast warn you about?

figure.title: Coastal forecast
lines: Visibility: moderate, poor in fog patches

options: Visibility will stay over 10 miles
In places you may see less than 1 km
Fog only over land, not at sea
Rain, with good visibility in between
questions.why: In forecasts 'fog' means visibility under 1000 m; 'poor' means under 2 miles.

questions.q: What will the afternoon be like?
options: A south-easterly wind, easing later
Rain showers and poor visibility
A stronger north-westerly and a rougher sea
Lighter wind and a calming sea
questions.why: 'Increasing 6 later' and 'becoming rough': more wind and bigger waves as the day goes on.

questions.q: What will this leg be like?
options: Calm — you will motor all the way
Downwind with the wind behind — easy
Wind on the beam — fast and comfortable
Upwind into wind and waves — slow and wet
questions.why: A north-easterly course into a north wind is close-hauled, at the windiest time of day.

questions.q: If the boat is still here at 15:00, which way is it being pushed?

figure.title: Lunch stop
lines: Anchored close off a south-facing beach

options: Towards the beach — the sea breeze blows onshore
Away from the beach — a land breeze blows out
Nowhere — it will stay calm all day
Along the beach — a westerly sets in
questions.why: The afternoon sea breeze blows onshore — off a south-facing beach it comes from the south.

questions.q: What do these signs together suggest?

figure.title: Watch log
lines: High wispy cloud thickening from the west
A long swell starting to arrive

options: Only a light shower, then sunshine
A depression with strong wind is approaching
A local sea breeze is about to start
A settled high is building over you
questions.why: Fast-falling pressure, thickening high cloud and a new swell all point to an approaching low.

questions.q: In the marina, the flag on the harbour office streams out towards the south-east. What wind is blowing?
options: A south-easterly
A south-westerly
A north-westerly
A north-easterly
questions.why: A flag streams downwind, so the wind comes from the opposite side — the north-west.

questions.q: Which Force on the Beaufort scale is this?
options: Force 8
Force 4
Force 5
Force 6
questions.why: Force 6 is 22–27 knots, a strong breeze.

questions.q: You are about to boil water on the galley stove. What is the right order?
options: Strike the match first, then open the burner
Open the burner, then look for the matches
Open all the burners, then light the one you need
Open the burner, wait a moment, then light it
questions.why: Have the flame ready first so no unburnt gas escapes — it sinks and collects in the bilge.

questions.q: You have finished cooking dinner at anchor. Besides closing the burner knob, what do you do?
options: Light the oven to burn off the spare gas
Turn the gas off at the solenoid or the bottle
Leave the bottle on, ready for breakfast
Just open a hatch to air the galley
questions.why: Shutting off at the source leaves no gas in the pipe to leak out overnight.

questions.q: You come down the companionway and notice this. How do you deal with it?

figure.title: Below, at anchor
lines: Faint smell of gas in the saloon

options: Switch on the cabin fan to clear the smell
Light the stove to find where it leaks
No flames or switches, gas off, tell the skipper
Start the engine to run the blower
questions.why: Bottled gas is heavier than air and pools low down — any spark can set it off.

questions.q: The skipper asks you to cook pasta while the boat sails heeled in a lively sea. How do you set up?
options: Gimbals locked, no strap, oilskin trousers on
Gimbals free, no strap, swimwear on
Gimbals locked, galley strap on, shorts on
Gimbals free, galley strap on, oilskin trousers on
questions.why: A swinging stove keeps pans level, the strap holds you, and clothing guards against scalds.

questions.q: On your first day aboard, a guest asks what can go down the marine toilet. What do you tell them?
options: Only what you have eaten, plus toilet paper
Anything small enough to fit the bowl
Wet wipes, if the pack says 'flushable'
Paper towels and cotton pads as well
questions.why: Marine heads block easily — everything else goes in the bin.

questions.q: You have used the heads and pumped until the bowl looks clean. What do you do next?
options: Pour in some bleach and close the lid
Keep pumping a while longer to clear the pipe
Close the lid and pump again tomorrow
Stop — a clean bowl means a clear pipe
questions.why: Waste still sits in the pipe after the bowl clears; extra strokes push it out to sea or the tank.

questions.q: You need to use the heads. What do you do first?
options: Use it, then pump extra sea water through
Use it as set — the outlet is well under water
Set the valve to the holding tank
Use it as it is — the tank is nearly empty
questions.why: In harbour, waste goes into the holding tank, never overboard.

questions.q: Under sail the skipper asks you to close the toilet seacocks after each use. Why?
options: So the toilet pump wears out less quickly
So the boat saves fresh water on passage
So smells from the tank stay out of the cabin
So sea water cannot siphon in and flood the boat
questions.why: When heeled, a toilet below the waterline can siphon sea water in through open seacocks.

questions.q: How do you help the water last?
options: Turn the tap off while you soap and scrub
Run the tap until the water comes out warm
Rinse the deck with fresh water each day
Shower as usual — the tanks will refill
questions.why: With no top-up, every litre counts: tap off while soaping, rinse sparingly.

questions.q: You are at anchor overnight with no shore power and the engine off. How do you help the batteries?
options: Leave the saloon lights on until morning
Switch off lights and chargers nobody is using
Charge all the phones and laptops overnight
Keep the fridge door open to cool the cabin
questions.why: With no charging, the house battery only holds what you save — switch off what you don't need.

questions.q: The skipper says 'stow everything, we sail in ten minutes'. Your laptop is on the saloon table. What do you do?
options: Move it onto the chart table instead
Leave it — the table has a raised edge
Put it in a locker or wedge it so it can't move
Put it on a cockpit seat to keep an eye on it
questions.why: When the boat heels, anything loose flies about — and breaks or hurts someone.

questions.q: What do you do about the hatch?

figure.title: Beating to windward
lines: Wind F5, spray coming over the bow
Forward cabin hatch open for air

options: Leave it — it is cooler with air below
Close it only if a wave comes right in
Close it halfway so some air still gets in
Close it now, before water comes below
questions.why: Hatches and portholes stay shut under way — one wave through the forehatch soaks the cabin.

questions.q: The skipper warns of a lumpy crossing tomorrow, and you get seasick easily. What do you do?
options: Take a tablet before you sail and skip the wine
Take a tablet once you start to feel sick
Stay up late so you sleep through the crossing
Eat a big greasy breakfast to settle your stomach
questions.why: Seasickness pills work best taken in advance; alcohol and tiredness make it worse.

questions.q: Halfway across, you start to feel queasy. Where is the best place for you?
options: At the chart table, checking the plotter
On deck in fresh air, watching the horizon
In the forward cabin, lying down
Below, reading to take your mind off it
questions.why: Fresh air and a steady horizon help; below decks, and above all forward, the motion is worst.

questions.q: After a sail change at anchor, sheets and halyard tails lie in a tangle across the cockpit floor. What do you do?
options: Kick them under the cockpit table
Leave them — they will be needed tomorrow
Coil them and stow them clear of feet
Drop them over the side to trail
questions.why: Loose lines trip people, and a line over the side can foul the propeller.

questions.q: At anchor, a guest is about to drop an empty plastic bottle over the side. What do you tell them?
options: Fine, if we are more than a mile offshore
Fine at night, when the beach is empty
Fine, as long as it is filled so it sinks
Keep it aboard and take it to the bins ashore
questions.why: Plastic never goes overboard: all rubbish stays aboard until you reach bins ashore.

questions.q: Roughly how much can each person use per day?

figure.title: Water check
lines: Three more days to the next marina

options: About 11 litres
About 66 litres
About 33 litres
About 3.5 litres
questions.why: 200 litres ÷ 6 people ÷ 3 days ≈ 11 litres each per day, cooking and washing included.

questions.q: With no charging, roughly how long until that is used up?

figure.title: House battery
lines: Anchor light and cabin lights: 2 A

options: About 25 hours
About 17 hours
About 50 hours
About 6 hours
questions.why: 4 A + 2 A = 6 A; 100 Ah ÷ 6 A ≈ 17 hours.

questions.q: How do you spend the next three hours?

figure.title: Night passage
lines: 21:00 — the others chat in the cockpit

options: Keep the helm company until your watch
Stay up with them and sleep after your watch
Go below and sleep, to be rested for midnight
Have a strong coffee so you stay awake later
questions.why: Off watch, sleep when you can — a tired watchkeeper misses things.

questions.q: What is the problem?

figure.title: Stove won't light
lines: Bottle valve in the gas locker: open
Solenoid switch on the panel: off
Burner open and match lit, no flame

options: The burner needs to stay open for longer
The gas locker lid has to be propped open
The bottle must be empty — change it now
The solenoid is off, so no gas reaches the stove
questions.why: With the solenoid off no gas flows: close the burner, switch the solenoid on, then light again.

questions.q: You see a crew member fall over the side. What do you do first?
options: Shout 'Man overboard!' and point at them
Start the engine before anything else
Go below to wake the skipper
Jump in after them straight away
questions.why: Raise the alarm and keep them in sight — a head in the waves is very easy to lose.

questions.q: The skipper makes you the spotter while the boat turns back. What is your job?

figure.note: Skipper turning the boat to come back

options: Point once, then help with the sheets
Point at the person and never look away
Fetch the first-aid kit from below
Call the coastguard on the VHF
questions.why: The spotter keeps eyes and an arm on the casualty until they are back alongside.

questions.q: Seconds after the shout of 'Man overboard!', you are next to the lifebuoy and danbuoy at the stern. What do you do?
options: Keep them aboard until the boat turns back
Wait for the skipper to tell you to throw
Throw them out towards the person at once
Throw them only once the person is close
questions.why: Thrown at once, they give the casualty something to hold and mark the spot.

questions.q: Why do you press the MOB button on the plotter now?

figure.title: Chart plotter
lines: Big red MOB button on the screen

options: It switches on all the deck lights
It stops the engine and the propeller
It sounds the horn to warn other boats
It marks the spot so you can steer back to it
questions.why: The plotter saves the position where the person went in and shows the way back.

questions.q: A pan of cooking oil catches fire on the stove. What do you do?
options: Turn off the gas and cover it with the fire blanket
Carry the pan out to the cockpit
Throw a cup of water over the flames
Spray it with the cockpit hose
questions.why: Smother a fat fire; water makes burning oil erupt out of the pan.

questions.q: Spilt diesel is burning in the bilge under the engine. Which do you reach for?
options: The deck wash hose on full
A powder extinguisher, aimed at the base
A towel to fan the flames down
A bucket of seawater thrown over it
questions.why: Never water on a fuel fire — it spreads the burning fuel. Use powder, CO2 or foam.

questions.q: A candle has set a bunk cushion smouldering in the forward cabin. Your friend says 'never use water on a boat fire'. Is she right here?
options: Yes — water is never used below decks
No — water is safe on any fire aboard
No — water is fine on burning fabric
Yes — water makes any fire spread
questions.why: Water suits solids such as fabric and wood; keep it off burning fat, fuel and wiring.

questions.q: You go below and find this. What do you do first?

figure.title: Below, under sail
lines: Skipper on deck at the helm

options: Bail quietly so as not to worry anyone
Call MAYDAY on the VHF straight away
Lift your bags onto the bunks to keep them dry
Tell the skipper, then help find where it comes in
questions.why: The skipper must know at once; finding the source matters more than pumping.

questions.q: Water is rising slowly in the bilge. You taste it: fresh, not salty. What does that suggest?
options: A leak from the fresh water tank or its pipes
A failed toilet seacock letting the sea in
Waves coming in through the cockpit drains
A hole in the hull below the waterline
questions.why: Fresh water means the boat's own system is leaking, not the sea coming in.

questions.q: The skipper is hurt and cannot use the radio; you must send a MAYDAY by voice. How do you set the VHF?
options: Channel 70, high power
Channel 16, high power
Channel 16, low power
The marina's working channel
questions.why: Distress voice calls go on channel 16, at full power for the best range.

questions.q: Under a flap on the VHF you find a red button marked DISTRESS. What does pressing and holding it do?
options: Turns on the strobe light at the masthead
Calls the nearest marina on its own channel
Sends an automatic alert with the boat's ID and position
Locks the radio on channel 16 for listening
questions.why: The DSC distress button sends a digital MAYDAY alert, with the GPS position if one is connected.

questions.q: After 'MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, this is yacht ORCA…', what do you say?
options: The boat's name again, until someone answers
The time, the weather and the sea state
Your names, home port and next harbour
Position, what is wrong, help needed, people aboard
questions.why: Where you are comes first, then the problem, the help you need and how many are aboard.

questions.q: How do you look after this crew member?
options: Shelter, dry clothes, blankets, a warm sweet drink
A hot shower straight away and a brandy
Rub their arms and legs hard to warm them
Leave them in wet clothes in the wind to dry
questions.why: Warm them gently: out of the wind, dry layers, a warm drink if alert — never alcohol.

questions.q: Boiling water from the kettle spills over a crew member's forearm. What do you do?
options: Spread butter or oil on it at once
Cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes
Pop the blisters so the skin can dry
Hold ice straight against the skin
questions.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes limits the burn; then cover it loosely with cling film.

questions.q: How do you look after Anna?

figure.title: Accidental gybe
lines: The boom hit Anna on the side of the head
Later: confused, asking the same thing

options: Put her on the helm to keep her busy
Give her painkillers and a cold beer
Keep her still, watch her and tell the skipper now
Let her sleep it off alone in her bunk
questions.why: Confusion after a blow to the head is a sign of serious injury — she needs watching and medical advice.

questions.q: How do you help your friend?

figure.title: Day two of a rough passage
lines: Your friend has been sick for 12 hours
Weak, dizzy, passing very little urine

options: Give her strong coffee to perk her up
Let her sleep — seasickness passes on its own
Give her a large glass of water in one go
Keep giving small sips and tell the skipper
questions.why: Long seasickness dehydrates: small frequent sips, and the skipper may need to get medical advice.

questions.q: What do you do for the helmsman?
options: Shade, lie down, cool with water, sip fluids
Strong coffee, then back to the helm
Move into full sun to sweat it out
Keep steering — it will pass by evening
questions.why: Heat exhaustion: get them cool and shaded and give fluids before it turns into heatstroke.

questions.q: A crew member collapses in the saloon. They are unconscious but breathing normally. How do you lay them while you wait for help?
options: Flat on their back, head on a pillow
On their side, in the recovery position
Face down, arms by their sides
Sitting up, propped against a bunk
questions.why: On their side the airway stays open and any vomit can drain out.

questions.q: A guest wants to get into the raft right now. When do you get in?

figure.title: Abandon ship?
lines: Yacht still afloat, water rising slowly

options: Now — a liferaft is always the safer place
Now, by jumping down into it from the deck
When the yacht is going down — step up into it
Once you have swum across to it
questions.why: Stay aboard as long as you can: you should step up into the raft as the yacht sinks.

questions.q: In what order do you act?

figure.title: Night, sailing, F4
lines: The skipper falls over the side
Only you and one guest aboard

options: Press MOB, call MAYDAY, then throw the buoys
Call MAYDAY, then shout, then throw the buoys
Turn the boat, then shout, throw the buoys
Shout, throw the buoys, press MOB, guest points
questions.why: Alarm, something to float on and a marked position come first — then the radio call.
